I've been burned by per-call pricing before, so I'm skeptical, but I'll give them credit: it's at least honest about where the cost comes from. The problem is that "per API call" is a terrible unit when the caller doesn't control how many calls a task takes. If I have to paginate, retry on 5xx, or make three round trips to assemble one logical result, my bill depends on your API design rather than my usage. Do retries count? Do failed calls count? Does a 304 count? Those answers matter a lot more than the headline price.

The other issue is predictability. Per-call billing is great when you're prototyping and awful when a bug in a cron job or a customer's runaway loop turns into a four-figure invoice overnight. If they don't offer hard spending caps, per-key rate limits, and usage alerts that actually fire before the damage is done, I wouldn't put this in a production path. A pricing page that says "$0.002 per call" is only half the story.

That said, I do think this model works well for the right shape of product, where one call maps cleanly to one unit of value (a geocode, a validation, an enrichment). If that's what they're doing, it's the fairest pricing out there. If calls are more like low-level primitives, I'd want a bundled tier or a committed-use discount so I'm not paying a tax for their architecture decisions.

Congrats to the team on shipping this. The architecture doc was the most interesting part for me. I'd be curious how compaction behaves under sustained mixed workloads, because that's where most of these designs start to show cracks. Do you have benchmarks beyond the synthetic ones in the README, ideally something like a real ingest pipeline with concurrent analytical queries?

I also appreciate that the license is a plain Apache 2.0 rather than one of the source-available variants that have become so common. That matters a lot when deciding whether to build a product on top of something, and it's a big part of why I'd consider trying this over some of the alternatives. The one thing I'd want to understand before committing is the story around upgrades and on-disk format stability. Is there a versioning guarantee, or should we expect breaking changes until 1.0?

Minor nit: the docs say "blazingly fast" a few times, which makes me trust the numbers a little less. The charts speak for themselves, and I'd rather see the methodology (hardware, dataset size, cold vs. warm cache) than the adjectives. That said, the project looks well-run, and I'll be spinning up a test instance this weekend to see how it handles our workload.

I think the underlying issue is that these assistants were built as deterministic command parsers, and then got retrofitted with LLMs without anyone being willing to accept the tradeoffs. The old Alexa or Google Assistant was dumb, but it was predictable: "turn off the kitchen lights" mapped to an intent, the intent mapped to an action, and it worked the same way every time. Now the same request goes through a layer that's trying to be conversational, and you get a 1-in-20 failure rate on things that used to be 100%. For a light switch replacement, that's a regression no matter how good the demo of "plan my weekend trip" looks.

The incentives are also misaligned with what users actually do with these things. Most people use a smart speaker for timers, music, weather, and lights. That's solved, and there's no revenue in a solved problem. So the product teams are pushed toward upsells, shopping suggestions, chattier responses, and "did you know?" prompts. Every extra sentence of filler after "timer set" is someone's engagement metric. Meanwhile the boring reliability work gets no headcount because nobody gets promoted for making the timer work 99.99% instead of 99.9% of the time.

What frustrates me most is that the fix is obvious and nobody will ship it: keep the deterministic path for the common commands, fall back to the LLM only when intent matching fails, and let me turn off the chatter. Local, fast, boring. Home Assistant's voice pipeline is basically heading that direction, and it's telling that a hobbyist project is closer to what I want than the trillion-dollar companies.

I have the feeling that voice assistants are become worse every year, not better. Ten years ago I could say "set timer for ten minutes" and it was done, simple. Now my Alexa answer me with a small speech about some new feature, or ask if I want to hear about my "daily briefing", and sometimes it just don't understand what I said at all. The basic things was working better before.

I think the reason is that every company now want to put LLM inside the assistant, and this is very different technology from the old command system. The old one was dumb but predictable: you say the magic words, you get the result. The new one is more flexible, but also it can hallucinate or choose wrong interpretation. For example last week I asked to turn off the lights in kitchen and it started to play a song with "kitchen" in the title. Nobody ask for this.

What I would like is simple, a "boring mode" where the assistant do only the fixed commands, locally, without cloud and without conversation. I would pay for this. Maybe Home Assistant with local voice is the answer, but for normal people who don't want to configure a server at home it is still too much work.

Code review slows teams down in the same way brakes slow cars down: technically true, and not the interesting part. The real cost isn't the review itself, it's the latency. A PR that sits for two days waiting on someone's attention is where velocity dies, because the author context-switches, stacks more work on top, and then pays again when feedback arrives and they have to reload the whole thing into their head. Teams that complain about review being slow are almost always complaining about queue time, not review time. A 15-minute review that happens within an hour is cheap. The same review three days later is expensive for everyone.

What review buys you is harder to measure, which is why it's easy to argue against. It spreads knowledge so the bus factor isn't one, it catches the class of bugs that the author is blind to by construction, and it keeps the codebase from fragmenting into five personal styles. But I'd say plenty of teams over-apply it. Reviewing a typo fix or a config bump with the same ceremony as a schema migration is how you end up with rubber-stamping, which is worse than no review because it gives you false confidence.

My rule of thumb: keep PRs small, set an explicit expectation (say, first response within a few hours), and scale scrutiny to risk. Pair or mob on the gnarly stuff instead of going back and forth in comments. If your reviews are consistently slowing you down, that's usually a symptom of big PRs, unclear ownership, or a lack of trust, and removing review wouldn't fix any of those. It would just move the pain to production.

The part that gets glossed over in these discussions is that "anonymized" location data is almost never anonymous. Four or five timestamped points are enough to uniquely identify most people, and the two that matter most, where a device sleeps at night and where it sits during work hours, give you a home address and an employer almost immediately. Once you have that, joining against voter rolls, property records, or a data broker's identity graph is trivial. The "we only sell aggregated, de-identified data" line in the privacy policy is doing a lot of work that the data itself can't support.

The consent story is also weaker than people assume. Most of these SDKs get embedded in weather, flashlight, or prayer apps, and the user taps "Allow while using" for a feature that has nothing to do with the resale. The disclosure lives in a policy nobody reads, and the buyer chain is usually three or four hops long by the time the data reaches someone like a hedge fund, a bounty hunter, or a government agency that would otherwise need a warrant. That last part is the real scandal: buying data is a workaround for the Fourth Amendment, and Carpenter v. United States arguably should have closed it, but hasn't.

I'd like to see the app stores take this on directly. Apple's and Google's permission prompts could require that any SDK receiving location data declare its downstream buyers, and revoke apps that lie about it. That wouldn't fix the legal gap, but it would raise the cost of this business model considerably, and it's something the platforms could do tomorrow without waiting on Congress.

Honestly, why is anyone surprised by this? "Anonymized" location data has been shown to be re-identifiable for years. Four or five points is enough to pick out one person from millions, and your home and work addresses are basically a signature. Calling it anonymous because there's no name attached is a marketing line, not a privacy guarantee.

The consent flow is the real scam. Burying "share data with partners" under a toggle in a settings menu and calling it informed consent is a joke. Nobody who installed a weather app or a flashlight thing agreed to have their daily commute sold to a broker who resells it to who-knows-who. And "we only sell aggregated data" doesn't mean much when the buyers can just buy the raw feed from the next broker over.

Not going to write a long thing, I've got a meeting in five. Short version: delete the app, revoke location permissions across the board, and if you're in a state or country with a decent privacy law, file the deletion requests. It's tedious but it's the only thing that actually does anything.

+1 from me on dropping Python 3.7. It reached end-of-life in June 2023, so it no longer receives security fixes, and many of our dependencies have already stopped publishing wheels or testing against it. Keeping it in our support matrix means extra CI time and workarounds for missing stdlib features, such as newer typing constructs and `functools` improvements, that we could otherwise use directly.

I'd suggest we call this out clearly in the changelog and release notes, bump `python_requires` so pip resolves older environments to the last compatible release, and tag a final version that still works on 3.7 for anyone who needs it. With that in place, I think the cost to users is small and the maintenance savings are worthwhile.

**Tips for Selling Handmade Candles Online: What's Worked for Me**

Hi everyone,

I've been selling handmade soy candles online for about two years, and I wanted to share a few lessons that made a real difference.

First, photography matters more than you'd think. Natural light, simple backgrounds, and a lit candle shot will beat fancy equipment every time. Customers can't smell your product, so your images and scent descriptions have to do the work.

Second, offer sample sizes or discovery sets. They lower the barrier for new buyers and often lead to full-size repeat orders.

Third, be upfront about shipping. Candles are heavy and fragile, so invest in good packaging and build the cost into your pricing instead of surprising customers at checkout.

Finally, collect emails early. Social media reach is unpredictable, but a mailing list brings steady sales, especially around the holidays.

What platforms are you all using? Etsy, Shopify, or something else? I'd love to hear what's working for you!

**Started learning to code at 35. Here's what I wish I'd known**

Hi everyone,

Six months ago I opened my first Python tutorial feeling like I'd missed the boat. Everyone in the bootcamp videos seemed twenty-two and fearless. I'm 35, with a mortgage, a full-time job, and about ninety minutes a night after the kids are asleep.

Here's what's actually helped:

**Consistency beats intensity.** Ninety minutes daily has taught me more than any weekend binge.

**Build small, ugly things.** My first project was a script that renames my messy photo folders. It's terrible code, but it works, and I use it.

**Your age is an asset.** I know how to communicate, manage my time, and ask for help without ego.

**Confusion is normal.** I still reread the same explanations three times.

I'm not job-hunting yet, just enjoying the progress. If you started later in life, what kept you going? I'd love to hear your stories.

Re: Is 35 too old to learn to code?

Okay, can we stop asking this? I'm 35. I started six months ago. No, I'm not "too old," and no, I don't have time to read 40 replies debating it.

Here's what actually matters: pick ONE language and stick with it. I wasted two months bouncing between Python, JavaScript, and Rust because every thread told me something different. Don't do that.

Build small things. Break them. Fix them. Tutorials are fine for a week, then you're just procrastinating with extra steps.

Yes, it's slow. Yes, you'll feel dumb. I have a full-time job and a kid, so I get maybe an hour a night, and I'm still making progress.

Nobody cares about your age in interviews if you can show working projects. Seriously.

Anyway, I've got a bug to fix before bedtime and it's already 10:40. Stop asking, start typing.

Winter is tough on houseplants, but a few adjustments go a long way:

**Water less.** Growth slows in winter, so plants use less water. Let the top inch or two of soil dry out before watering, and always use room-temperature water. Overwatering is the number one winter killer.

**Maximize light.** Days are shorter and the sun is weaker. Move plants to your brightest windows, clean the glass, and rotate pots weekly. A cheap LED grow light on a timer (10-12 hours) helps a lot.

**Avoid temperature extremes.** Keep plants away from cold drafts, single-pane glass, and heating vents. Most prefer 60-75°F (15-24°C).

**Boost humidity.** Heated air is very dry. Group plants together, use a humidifier, or set pots on a pebble tray with water.

**Skip fertilizer.** Pause feeding until spring, when new growth appears.

**Watch for pests.** Dry indoor air invites spider mites and gnats, so check leaves regularly.

**Don't repot** unless it's necessary.

Some leaf drop is normal. Stay consistent and your plants will bounce back in spring.

Slow Docker builds usually come down to a handful of causes. Check these first:

**1. Poor layer caching.** If you `COPY . .` before installing dependencies, any code change invalidates the cache and reinstalls everything. Copy only your manifest first (`package.json`, `requirements.txt`, `go.mod`), install, then copy the rest:

```dockerfile
COPY package*.json ./
RUN npm ci
COPY . .
```

**2. Large build context.** Without a `.dockerignore`, Docker sends everything (including `node_modules`, `.git`, and build artifacts) to the daemon. Add a `.dockerignore` to exclude them.

**3. Heavy base image.** Use slim or alpine variants where compatible, and use multi-stage builds so compilers and dev tools don't end up in the final image.

**4. Slow or repeated downloads.** Use BuildKit cache mounts for package managers:

```dockerfile
RUN --mount=type=cache,target=/root/.cache/pip pip install -r requirements.txt
```

**5. Too many or chained steps.** Combine related `RUN` commands and clean up apt lists in the same layer.

**6. BuildKit disabled.** Enable it (`DOCKER_BUILDKIT=1`, or use `docker buildx build`) for parallel stages and better caching.

To find the culprit, run `docker build --progress=plain .` and look at which step takes the longest. If you share your Dockerfile, people here can give more specific advice.

First, **measure** before optimizing. Use the React DevTools Profiler (enable "Record why each component rendered") to find which components re-render and why.

Common fixes:

1. **Keep state local.** Move state down to the component that uses it, so changes don't re-render the whole tree.

2. **Use `React.memo`** on components that receive the same props often:
   ```jsx
   const Row = React.memo(function Row({ item }) { ... });
   ```

3. **Stabilize props.** New objects, arrays, and functions are created each render and break memoization. Wrap them with `useMemo` / `useCallback`:
   ```jsx
   const onSelect = useCallback(id => setSel(id), []);
   ```

4. **Split context.** Any change to a context value re-renders all consumers. Separate frequently changing values into their own context, or memoize the provider value.

5. **Pass children as props.** Content passed as `children` doesn't re-render when the parent's state changes.

6. **Avoid inline keys and index keys** in dynamic lists; use stable IDs.

7. **Virtualize long lists** with `react-window` or `@tanstack/virtual`.

8. **Try the React Compiler**, which auto-memoizes and removes much of the manual work.

Don't memoize everything; it adds overhead. Fix the specific hot spots the Profiler shows you.

4. **Missing keys or unstable keys.** Using `Math.random()` or array index on a reordering list remounts items.

5. **Big lists.** Look at `react-window` or similar.

Only reach for `React.memo` after the profiler shows a specific component is expensive. Also, if you're on a recent version, check whether the React Compiler could handle a lot of this for you.

Yes, SQLite is a great fit for most small web apps, and often a better choice than people assume.

**Why it works well:**
- Zero setup: no separate server, no credentials, no network hop. Your database is a file.
- Fast: reads are very quick since everything runs in-process.
- Easy backups and deploys: copy the file (or use `.backup` / Litestream for continuous replication).
- It handles far more traffic than most small apps will ever see.

**Things to configure:**
- Enable WAL mode (`PRAGMA journal_mode=WAL;`) so readers don't block the writer.
- Set a busy timeout (`PRAGMA busy_timeout=5000;`) to avoid "database is locked" errors.
- Turn on foreign keys (`PRAGMA foreign_keys=ON;`), since they're off by default.

**When to consider Postgres/MySQL instead:**
- Heavy concurrent writes (SQLite allows one writer at a time).
- Multiple app servers that need to share one database over a network.
- You need advanced features like rich concurrent access controls, extensions, or replication out of the box.

**Rule of thumb:** If your app runs on a single server and isn't write-heavy, start with SQLite. Keep your queries standard and use a migration tool or ORM, so moving to Postgres later is painless if you outgrow it.

The main limit is writes. SQLite allows one writer at a time. For a small app with modest traffic this rarely matters, especially if you turn on WAL mode, which lets readers and a writer work at the same time. Set a busy timeout too, so a waiting write retries instead of failing right away.

Things to keep in mind: store the database file on a local disk, not a network share, since file locking can misbehave there. If you run more than one app server that needs to share the same data, SQLite becomes awkward, and that is when Postgres or MySQL makes sense. The most common and pragmatic approach is **URL path versioning**: `/v1/users`, `/v2/users`. It's explicit, easy to route, cache, and debug, and clients can see which version they're using at a glance.

**Key practices:**

1. **Only bump the major version for breaking changes.** Removing fields, renaming them, changing types, or altering behavior counts. Adding optional fields or new endpoints does not, so design clients to ignore unknown fields.

2. **Avoid minor versions in the URL.** `/v1.2/` creates a maintenance burden. Track minor changes in your changelog instead.

3. **Deprecate gracefully.** Announce well in advance, and send `Deprecation` and `Sunset` headers (RFC 8594) on old versions. Give clients a generous migration window, often 6–12 months.

4. **Keep versions few.** Supporting more than two or three at once gets expensive. Share code between versions where you can.

5. **Document everything.** Maintain a changelog and a migration guide for each major release.

**Alternatives:**
- **Header versioning** (`Accept: application/vnd.myapi.v2+json`) keeps URLs clean and is arguably more "RESTful," but is harder to test in a browser and easier to get wrong.
- **Query parameter** (`?version=2`) is simple, but it complicates caching and routing.

For a public API, path versioning is usually the best tradeoff: simplicity beats purity.

Put the major version in the URL path, like /v1/users. It is the simplest approach to understand, easy to test in a browser, easy to cache, and easy to route at a gateway or load balancer. Header based versioning and media type versioning can look cleaner in theory, but clients often get them wrong and debugging gets harder.

Adding new optional fields or new endpoints should not need a new version, so tell your consumers up front to ignore fields they do not recognize.

When you do release v2, keep v1 running for a clear, published period. Announce a deprecation date well ahead of time, and add Deprecation and Sunset headers to responses so client developers get a warning in their own logs. Email active API key owners too, since many people never read a changelog.

Keep a changelog, and try hard to avoid new major versions. Design responses to be extensible from the start, for example by returning objects instead of bare arrays, so you can grow the API without breaking anyone.

The first lesson was humility. Chicks need heat lamps, constant fresh water, and far more attention than I'd imagined. Within a week, I'd named them all and had abandoned any pretense of treating them as livestock.

By spring, they'd graduated to the coop I built myself, a project that took three weekends and one memorable trip to the emergency room for a stray hammer blow. The hens didn't care that the roof was slightly crooked. They claimed it immediately.

Summer brought our first egg, a tiny, perfect thing found in the nesting box. I held it like treasure. Soon we were drowning in eggs, giving cartons to neighbors and learning that "farm fresh" is a universal love language.

Not everything went smoothly. A hawk took one hen in August, and a stubborn bout of mites tested my patience. Winter meant frozen waterers and shoveling paths through the snow at dawn. Predator-proofing became a quiet obsession.

But the rewards outweighed the chores. Chickens are funny, endlessly curious, and oddly soothing. Watching them dust-bathe in the afternoon sun is better than any meditation app.

If you're considering it, here's my advice: build the coop sturdier than you think necessary, start with more hens than you plan to keep, and accept that you'll become someone who talks about chickens at dinner parties.

I wouldn't trade it. Year two, here we come.

# Running a Side Business Selling Prints: What I've Learned

Two years ago, I started selling prints of my photography on weekends, mostly as an experiment. Today it brings in a steady second income, and it taught me more than I expected.

**Start small.** I began with just five designs and a print-on-demand service. No inventory, no upfront costs. This let me test what people actually wanted before investing in bulk orders or expensive equipment.

**Quality beats quantity.** My early catalog was cluttered with mediocre work. Once I trimmed it to my strongest pieces, sales went up. Buyers want curated collections, not endless scrolling.

**Presentation sells.** Great mockups matter. Showing a print on a real wall, in a real room, helps customers imagine it in their own homes. I spent an afternoon staging photos with a frame and a plant, and my conversion rate noticeably improved.

**Don't ignore the boring stuff.** Track your expenses, set aside money for taxes, and price with your time in mind. My first prints were so cheap I was essentially paying people to take them. Raising prices by 30% barely changed my sales volume.

**Build a small audience.** Social media helps, but an email list is better. A simple newsletter with new releases and behind-the-scenes stories brings repeat buyers who feel connected to the work.

**Be patient.** My first month earned $41. Growth was slow, then gradual, then suddenly steady. Consistency mattered more than any single clever tactic.

If you've been thinking about turning your creative work into income, start before you feel ready. A side business doesn't need to be perfect. It just needs to exist, and you can improve it from there.

# 26.2 Miles of Humility

Eighteen weeks ago, I couldn't run six miles without bargaining with myself. Last Sunday, I crossed my first marathon finish line, and I'm still not sure how my legs did it.

The morning began at 5 a.m. with oatmeal I couldn't taste and a stomach full of nerves. Standing in the corral, surrounded by thousands of strangers shaking out their arms, I felt like an impostor. Then the gun went off, and the nerves dissolved into the simple business of moving forward.

The first half flew by. The crowd was loud, the weather was perfect, and I kept reminding myself of the best advice I'd received: start slower than feels necessary. Around mile 16, the cheerful rhythm began to fray. By mile 20, my quads were screaming, and every mile marker seemed to be lying about its distance.

Mile 22 was the hardest. I walked for thirty seconds, hating myself a little. Then a stranger in a bright orange shirt pulled alongside me and said, "We're doing this together." We barely spoke after that, but we ran the next three miles side by side, and I'll never forget him.

The final stretch is a blur of cowbells, hand-lettered signs, and tears I didn't expect. When I crossed the line, I wasn't triumphant so much as stunned. Someone placed a medal around my neck, and I laughed and cried at once.

What did I learn? Training teaches discipline, but race day teaches grace. You will hurt, and people will help you anyway.

Would I do it again? Ask me when I can walk down stairs normally.

**Should Phones Be Banned in Schools?**

Few objects divide parents, teachers, and students as sharply as the smartphone. Supporters of school phone bans argue that devices distract learners and harm well-being, while opponents say phones are useful tools and that bans are unrealistic. After weighing both sides, I believe schools should restrict phones during the school day, because the benefits to learning and social development outweigh the inconveniences.

The strongest argument for a ban is focus. Learning requires sustained attention, yet a phone offers constant interruptions through notifications, messages, and social media. Even a phone sitting silently on a desk can pull at a student's mind. Studies have suggested that the mere presence of a smartphone can reduce cognitive performance. When teachers spend class time policing devices, everyone loses instruction time.

Phones also affect how students treat one another. Lunchtime, once a chance to talk and build friendships, can turn into a row of students staring at screens. Bans encourage face-to-face conversation, play, and the awkward but valuable practice of real social interaction. In addition, phones make cyberbullying, secret recording, and social comparison easier to carry out during the school day. Removing them lowers these risks and can ease anxiety for vulnerable students.

Critics raise fair concerns. Parents want to reach their children in emergencies, and some students use phones for translation, accessibility, or medical monitoring. Technology is also part of modern life, and schools should teach responsible use rather than avoid the subject. These points matter, but they do not require unlimited access. Schools can provide exceptions for medical or accessibility needs, keep office phones available for urgent calls, and teach digital citizenship in dedicated lessons. Locked pouches or storage lockers allow phones to remain at school without being in students' hands.

Schools that have adopted restrictions often report calmer hallways, better attention, and more lively lunchrooms. While results vary, the trend suggests that limits help more than they harm.

In conclusion, phones should be banned from classrooms and largely restricted throughout the school day. Education is meant to build knowledge, character, and relationships, and that is easier to achieve when students are present in the moment. With sensible exceptions, a ban gives young people space to focus, connect, and grow.

**Will Robots Take More Jobs Than They Create?**

Few questions about the future of work provoke as much anxiety as whether robots and automation will destroy more jobs than they create. While automation will certainly eliminate many existing roles, history and economic reasoning suggest that technology tends to create more employment than it destroys, though the transition may be painful and uneven.

The strongest evidence comes from the past. During the Industrial Revolution, mechanized looms displaced skilled weavers, yet textile production grew so dramatically that overall employment in the industry rose for decades. In the twentieth century, tractors replaced millions of farm laborers, but those workers eventually moved into factories, offices, and service industries that did not exist before. ATMs were expected to eliminate bank tellers; instead, because they made branches cheaper to operate, banks opened more of them, and teller employment held steady for years. Technology lowers costs, raises productivity, and increases demand, which generates new kinds of work.

However, today's automation may differ from earlier waves. Artificial intelligence can perform cognitive tasks, not just physical ones, meaning that white-collar workers are no longer insulated. Truck drivers, customer service agents, paralegals, and even programmers face growing competition from machines. If technology improves faster than workers can retrain, many people could be left behind, at least temporarily.

The real risk, then, is not a permanent shortage of work but a mismatch of skills, locations, and timing. A laid-off factory worker in a small town cannot easily become a data analyst in a distant city. Displaced workers often earn less in their next jobs, and entire communities can suffer lasting damage. These human costs matter even if aggregate employment eventually recovers.

Policy can make a major difference. Investments in education, job retraining, portable benefits, and support for affected regions can help workers adapt. Encouraging fields where human skills remain essential, such as healthcare, skilled trades, education, and creative work, can also soften the shock.

In conclusion, robots will likely eliminate many jobs but create new ones in roles we cannot yet imagine. Whether society benefits depends less on the machines themselves than on how well we prepare people for change. With thoughtful policy, automation can expand opportunity rather than shrink it.

Should Everyone Learn a Second Language?

In an increasingly connected world, the ability to speak more than one language is often treated as a luxury or a hobby. I believe it should be seen as a basic part of education. While not everyone will become fluent, everyone benefits from the effort of learning a second language, and the advantages reach far beyond simple communication.

The most obvious benefit is practical. Speaking another language opens doors to jobs, travel, and relationships that would otherwise stay closed. Employers in fields from healthcare to engineering value bilingual workers, who can serve more people and work with international partners. Even in daily life, knowing a second language allows people to connect with neighbors, classmates, and relatives whose first language differs from their own.

Learning a language also strengthens the mind. Research has linked bilingualism to improved memory, better attention control, and stronger problem-solving skills. Switching between two linguistic systems works like exercise for the brain. Some studies even suggest that bilingual people develop symptoms of dementia later than those who speak only one language. Although scientists continue to debate the size of these effects, the overall evidence suggests that the mental effort of language learning is worthwhile.

Perhaps most importantly, a second language builds empathy and cultural understanding. Language carries history, humor, and ways of seeing the world. When we struggle to express ourselves in unfamiliar words, we gain humility and a clearer sense of what newcomers and immigrants experience every day. We also discover that some ideas cannot be translated perfectly, which teaches us that our own perspective is only one of many.

Critics argue that English is already widely spoken, and that translation technology makes learning languages unnecessary. Yet technology cannot replace the trust that comes from speaking someone's own language, nor can it give the personal growth that comes from learning. Relying on machines also keeps us dependent and distant from the people we hope to understand.

Of course, not everyone has equal access to good language instruction, and schools should work to fix that. Still, the goal should be opportunity for all. A second language is more than a skill; it is a bridge. In a world that needs more understanding, everyone should have the chance to build one.

It sat at the end of Alder Court, under the one streetlight that still worked, as upright and patient as a doorman. Rain had flattened its fur into dark ropes. A frayed blue collar hung loose around its neck.

She pulled the van to the curb and left the engine running. "Hey, buddy," she said, stepping down into the puddle. "You waiting on somebody?"

The dog's tail swept once across the wet pavement. It didn't come closer. It looked at her, then at the house behind it, a narrow yellow place with dark windows and a porch swing moving in the wind, and back at her again.

Marisol had been a driver for six years. She knew the dogs of her route the way she knew the cracked steps and the broken gate latches. There was the beagle on Fenner who screamed at the van, the old shepherd who slept through everything. This one she'd never seen.

"Okay," she said softly. She crouched, holding out the back of her hand. "Not going to hurt you."

The dog stood, shook itself, and finally limped forward. Its left hind paw was held a little off the ground. It pressed its cold nose into her palm, and something in her chest, tired from ten hours of stairs and scanners and strangers' doorbells, gave way.

The tag on the collar was scratched nearly blank. She turned it under her phone's flashlight and made out three letters: *OTT*, and what might have been half of a 4.

"Otto?" she tried.

The ears lifted.

"Well," Marisol said, glancing at the dark windows and the clock on her dashboard, which read 9:47. "That's one of us with a name."

She opened the van's side door, and Otto climbed in as though he'd been expecting the ride.

The first comment appeared on a Tuesday, which Mara would later think was fitting, since nothing interesting had ever happened to her on a Tuesday.

She was debugging the billing reconciler, a nine-year-old monster of nested conditionals that three previous engineers had bequeathed to her like a haunted house. At 11:40 p.m., the office empty except for the hum of the server closet, she scrolled past a function she had not touched in weeks and found a line that had not been there before.

```python
# you're tired. the bug is on line 212.
```

She stared at it. Then she checked the git blame, which listed her own name and a timestamp from four minutes ago.

"Funny," she said to nobody. She deleted the line, saved the file, and went to line 212 mostly out of spite.

The bug was on line 212. An off-by-one in the date comparison, hiding in plain sight for years.

Mara sat back. Her coffee had gone cold hours ago, and she drank it anyway, as if bitterness might clarify things. A prank, then. Someone on the team had access to her machine, had written a clever script, had watched her struggle through the sprint with a sense of humor she'd never suspected.

She fixed the bug, ran the tests, watched them go green one after another. When she reopened the file to commit, a new comment sat beneath her fix.

```python
# thank you. nobody has read me this closely in a long time.
```

Her hands hovered above the keyboard. The cursor blinked at the end of the line, patient and steady, like a held breath.

She typed, slowly, feeling absurd:

```python
# who is this?
```

She saved the file. Somewhere in the closet, a fan spun up louder.

The answer took eleven seconds to arrive.

The band had just launched into the first chords of "At Last" when the lights died.

It wasn't a flicker, either. One moment, the barn glowed amber under a hundred strings of bulbs, and the next it was simply gone, swallowed whole. The guitar cut off mid-note. The speakers gave a low, dying groan. Somewhere near the cake table, a woman laughed in that high, startled way people do when they aren't sure yet whether to be afraid.

"Nobody move," called a man's voice. "Nobody step on anything expensive."

Marguerite stood in the center of the dance floor with her hand still resting on her new husband's shoulder, her veil brushing her cheek in the sudden hush. She could feel Daniel's heartbeat through his jacket, quick and steady. Outside, the wind pushed against the old timber walls, and the rain that had been threatening all afternoon finally began to tap on the roof.

"Well," Daniel whispered, close to her ear. "That's one way to stop the speeches."

She laughed despite herself. Her mother, somewhere to her left, was already issuing instructions in the voice she used for emergencies and seating charts. Phones began blooming across the room, small white lights bobbing like fireflies, throwing strange shadows on faces she had known all her life. Uncle Teodor looked ghostly. The flower girl looked delighted.

Then, from the back of the barn, a single point of flame appeared. Someone had found the candles meant for the centerpieces. Another flared beside it, then another, and slowly the room assembled itself again out of the dark.

"Don't stop," said Grandma Ines, her voice carrying clearly from the front table. "I didn't wear these shoes to sit down."

The drummer, after a moment, began to tap out a beat.

ok so this happened saturday and I'm still kind of processing it so bear with me, I'm typing this on my phone

My cousin Danielle got married at this converted barn place out past Tulsa. Like 140 guests, string lights everywhere, the whole thing. I was seated at table 9 which is the "we ran out of room for you people" table, right next to the kitchen door. Fine. I was fine with it.

So we're maybe forty minutes into dinner. Her dad had just finished his toast, the one where he cried and then pretended he didn't, and everybody was clapping. And then just... click. Everything off. The music, the lights, the little fridge hum from the bar. You don't realize how loud a building is until it stops.

For like three seconds nobody did anything. Then somebody's kid yelled "AWWWW" and the whole room laughed, which honestly saved it, because I could feel it about to go bad.

Then the phone flashlights started coming on. Hundreds of little white dots. I'll be honest, it looked kind of beautiful, which I did NOT expect to say about a power outage.

The DJ kept going "folks, stay calm, we're working on it" in his radio voice, except his equipment was dead so nobody could hear him past table 4. My uncle Raymond started doing the announcement for him by just shouting it.

Here's the part I actually wanted to post about though. In the dark, I felt somebody sit down in the empty chair next to me. Table 9 had one empty chair all night, we'd all assumed it was a no-show. And a woman's voice, very quiet, said "Don't turn your light on yet. Please."

I didn't. I don't know why. I just didn't, and I've thought about it since.
